title: The Kingdom Divides
summary: After Solomon, the ten northern tribes secede — Israel in the north, Judah in the south — and the story runs on two tracks.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** After Solomon's death his son Rehoboam threatens even heavier burdens than his father's, and the northern tribes secede under Jeroboam (1 Kings 12). The kingdom splits in two: **Israel** in the north (ten tribes, its capital eventually Samaria) and **Judah** in the south (Jerusalem, the temple, the line of David). The prophet Ahijah had foretold it, tearing his robe into twelve pieces as a sign (1 Kings 11:29–31). From here the biblical narrative runs on two tracks, and the books of Kings judge every king of each kingdom by a single measure: faithfulness to the LORD.

**Register and history.** The division (conventionally 931 BC) is roughly where the biblical narrative enters far better-attested territory — from here Israelite and Judean kings begin to appear in Assyrian, Babylonian, and Moabite records. This entry is marked *attested* for the divided-monarchy framework, even as individual early episodes vary in corroboration.

**Why it matters.** The northern kingdom will fall to Assyria and vanish; the southern kingdom of Judah — carrying David's line and the temple — will fall to Babylon but return. The gold thread of promise runs down the southern, Davidic track.
readingPointer: Read the split in 1 Kings 12.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on 1 Kings 12
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Israel"
Diarmaid MacCulloch, Christianity: The First Three Thousand Years

title: Jeroboam I
summary: First king of the breakaway north, who set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan — the archetype of the faithless king.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Jeroboam son of Nebat, an official under Solomon, is told by the prophet Ahijah that he will rule ten tribes; after Solomon's death he leads the northern secession and becomes the first king of Israel (1 Kings 11–12). To keep his people from going up to worship in Jerusalem, he sets up two golden calves, at Bethel and Dan, with a rival priesthood and festival (1 Kings 12:25–33). For this the books of Kings brand him the archetype of the bad king: nearly every northern ruler after him is condemned for walking "in the sins of Jeroboam."

**Register and dating.** Jeroboam I reigned c. 931–910 BC on the conventional reckoning; the northern kingdom he founds becomes well-attested within a century, though Jeroboam himself is not directly named outside scripture (marked *traditional*).

**His emblem.** The golden calves deliberately echo the calf at Sinai — the emblem returns here to mark the same sin repeated at the founding of the northern kingdom.
readingPointer: His story is told in 1 Kings 11–14.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on 1 Kings 12–14
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Jeroboam"

title: Ahab & Jezebel
summary: The king of Israel and his Phoenician queen who promoted Baal — provoking Elijah, and Naboth's judicial murder.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Ahab, king of Israel, marries Jezebel, a Phoenician princess, and under her promotes the worship of Baal, provoking the great confrontation with the prophet Elijah — the contest on Mount Carmel, where the LORD answers with fire (1 Kings 18). Jezebel hunts the prophets of the LORD and, in the story of Naboth's vineyard, has an innocent man judicially murdered so Ahab can seize his land (1 Kings 21). Both come to violent ends foretold by Elijah.

**What history can say.** Ahab is solidly attested: Assyrian records (the Kurkh Monolith) name him among the kings who fought Shalmaneser III at the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC, fielding a large chariot force, and the Moabite Mesha Stele refers to the Omride dynasty. This entry is marked *attested*. The Baal cult he and Jezebel promoted, and the prophetic resistance to it, are the theological heart of the narrative.

**Their long shadow.** "Jezebel" becomes a byword — for idolatry and ruthless power — down to the New Testament (Revelation 2:20).
readingPointer: Their story runs from 1 Kings 16 through 2 Kings 9.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on 1 Kings 16–22
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Ahab"
Diarmaid MacCulloch, Christianity: The First Three Thousand Years

title: Elijah
summary: The prophet of fire who faced down Baal on Mount Carmel and was taken up in a whirlwind — the type of the prophet to come.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Elijah the Tishbite bursts into the story to announce a drought against Ahab's Baal-worshiping kingdom (1 Kings 17). He is fed by ravens, raises a widow's son, and on Mount Carmel calls down fire from heaven to expose Baal as nothing (1 Kings 18); then, exhausted and despairing, he meets God not in wind, earthquake, or fire but in "a low whisper" (1 Kings 19:12). He confronts Ahab over Naboth's vineyard, anoints his successor Elisha, and at the end is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, a chariot of fire dividing him from Elisha (2 Kings 2).

**Register and dating.** Elijah belongs to the 9th century BC, the reign of Ahab; he is not attested outside scripture, and his narratives blend prophetic legend and history (marked *traditional*).

**His long reach.** Elijah becomes the type of the prophet who is to come: Malachi promises he will return before "the great and awesome day of the LORD" (Malachi 4:5), the Gospels connect that role with John the Baptist, and Elijah himself appears with Moses at the Transfiguration (Mark 9:4) — the Prophets beside the Law.
readingPointer: His story runs from 1 Kings 17 through 2 Kings 2.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on 1 Kings 17 – 2 Kings 2
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Elijah"

title: Elisha
summary: Elijah's successor, who took up the fallen mantle and a double portion of his spirit — the prophet of mercy and provision.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Elisha, plowing when Elijah casts his mantle over him, leaves everything to follow (1 Kings 19:19–21). When Elijah is taken up, Elisha catches the falling mantle and asks a double portion of his spirit; his ministry is a stream of wonders — the widow's oil, the healing of Naaman the Syrian's leprosy, the floating axe head, the raising of the Shunammite's son, food multiplied (2 Kings 2–13). Where Elijah is fire and confrontation, Elisha is more often mercy and provision.

**Register and dating.** Elisha belongs to the 9th–8th century BC; like Elijah he is not attested outside scripture (marked *traditional*).

**His place in the story.** He is the successor prophet — the mantle passed on — and his miracles of healing and feeding are echoed in the Gospels' portrait of Jesus.
readingPointer: His story runs from 2 Kings 2 through 2 Kings 13.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on 2 Kings 2–13
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Elisha"

title: Amos
summary: The shepherd of Tekoa sent north to thunder against injustice — "let justice roll down like waters."
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Amos, a shepherd and fig-farmer of Tekoa in Judah — "no prophet, nor a prophet's son" (7:14) — is sent north to prosperous Israel to thunder against injustice: the selling of the poor "for a pair of sandals," the trampling of the needy, worship God hates while the courts are corrupt. "Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream" (5:24). God shows him a plumb line held against a wall that has gone out of true.

**Register and dating.** Amos prophesied c. 760–750 BC, an older contemporary of Hosea; thinly corroborated outside scripture (marked *traditional*).

**His long reach.** Amos is the great prophet of social justice, his words carried across the centuries — by the early church, and famously by Martin Luther King Jr.
readingPointer: Read the book of Amos — nine short chapters.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introduction to Amos
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Amos"

title: Hosea
summary: The prophet whose own marriage to an unfaithful wife became a picture of God's love for faithless Israel.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Hosea prophesies to the northern kingdom in its last decades, and his own marriage is his message: God tells him to marry Gomer, who proves unfaithful, and to love her still — a living picture of the LORD's love for faithless Israel (Hosea 1–3). His words swing between heartbroken judgment and tender mercy: "When Israel was a child, I loved him" (11:1); "I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice" (6:6).

**Register and dating.** Hosea prophesied in the mid-8th century BC, before the fall of Samaria; thinly corroborated outside scripture (marked *traditional*).

**His long reach.** Hosea gives the Bible its deepest image of covenant as marriage — taken up by the prophets, by Jesus, and by Paul; Matthew reads "out of Egypt I called my son" (11:1) as fulfilled in Christ.
readingPointer: Read the marriage sign in Hosea 1–3.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introduction to Hosea
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Hosea"

title: Jonah
dateDisplay: the prophet 8th century BC; the book's date & genre debated
summary: The prophet who fled God's call to merciful Nineveh, was swallowed by a great fish, and sulked when the city repented.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Jonah is sent to preach to Nineveh, the capital of cruel Assyria, and flees the other way by sea; thrown overboard in a storm, he is swallowed by a great fish, prays from its belly, and is delivered to try again. When Nineveh actually repents, Jonah sulks — he wanted judgment, not mercy — and God rebukes his hard heart with a withered plant and a question about pity (Jonah 4). A real prophet, Jonah son of Amittai, is named in 2 Kings 14:25 (8th century BC).

**Register, and a genuine question of genre.** How to read the book of Jonah is debated: some take it as historical narrative, many as a deliberate parable or satire — a didactic story about God's mercy reaching even Israel's enemies. Its date of composition is likewise uncertain (often placed after the exile). This entry is marked *contested* to hold that open question of genre and history; the book's *point* — that God's compassion is wider than his people's — is not in doubt.

**Its long reach.** Jesus makes "the sign of Jonah" — three days in the fish — a figure of his own death and resurrection (Matthew 12:39–41).
readingPointer: Read the book of Jonah — only four chapters.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introduction to Jonah
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Jonah, Book of"

title: Isaiah
dateDisplay: 8th century BC (the prophet; book's authorship debated)
summary: The prophet of Immanuel and the suffering servant — the most quoted prophet in the New Testament.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Isaiah of Jerusalem is called in the year King Uzziah died, in a vision of the LORD high and lifted up, his unclean lips touched with a burning coal (Isaiah 6). For decades he counsels the kings of Judah — above all Hezekiah, whom he strengthens as Assyria besieges Jerusalem (Isaiah 36–37). His book holds the Old Testament's most soaring visions of judgment and hope: the child called Immanuel (7:14), the government upon the shoulders of a coming king (9:6), swords beaten into plowshares (2:4), and the suffering servant "wounded for our transgressions" (53:5).

**Register, and a note on the book.** Isaiah the prophet belongs to the 8th century BC (marked *traditional*). The authorship of the book is a major scholarly question — many hold that chapters 40–66, addressed to exiles in Babylon two centuries later, come from later hands within Isaiah's tradition ("Second" and "Third" Isaiah), while others defend its unity. This project reports that debate rather than settling it; it belongs fully to the book's own entry.

**His long reach.** No prophet is quoted more in the New Testament; the Gospels and Handel alike reach for Isaiah to say who Jesus is.
readingPointer: Read his call in Isaiah 6, and the servant song in Isaiah 53.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introduction to Isaiah
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Isaiah"

title: Micah
summary: Contemporary of Isaiah, who named Bethlehem's coming ruler and summed up true religion: do justice, love mercy, walk humbly.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Micah of Moresheth, a contemporary of Isaiah, prophesies to both kingdoms, denouncing the powerful who "covet fields and seize them" while promising restoration. His book holds two of scripture's most famous lines: the vision of nations beating swords into plowshares and learning war no more (4:3), and the summary of true religion — "to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God" (6:8). He names Bethlehem as the birthplace of a coming ruler (5:2).

**Register and dating.** Micah prophesied in the late 8th century BC; thinly corroborated outside scripture (marked *traditional*).

**His long reach.** Matthew cites Micah's Bethlehem prophecy at the birth of Jesus (Matthew 2:5–6), and Micah 6:8 is among the most-quoted verses on justice and humility in either Testament.
readingPointer: Read Micah 5–6.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introduction to Micah
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Micah"

title: Fall of the Northern Kingdom
summary: Assyria destroys Samaria and deports Israel — the ten northern tribes scattered and, in history, largely lost.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** The northern kingdom of Israel, after two centuries of mostly faithless kings, falls to the Assyrian empire: Samaria is besieged and taken, and its people are deported and scattered across the empire, replaced by foreign settlers (2 Kings 17). The biblical historian gives the theological verdict plainly — Israel fell because it had forsaken the LORD (2 Kings 17:7–23). The ten northern tribes, exiled and assimilated, largely vanish from history (the "lost tribes").

**What history confirms.** This is firm history: Assyrian royal inscriptions (of Shalmaneser V and Sargon II) record the fall of Samaria in 722/721 BC and the deportation, matching the biblical account closely. Marked *attested*.

**Its meaning.** The fall of the north is a warning held up before Judah for the next 136 years — and one Judah largely fails to heed, until Babylon comes.
readingPointer: Read the fall and its verdict in 2 Kings 17.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on 2 Kings 17
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Samaria"
Diarmaid MacCulloch, Christianity: The First Three Thousand Years

title: Hezekiah
summary: One of Judah's great reforming kings, delivered from Assyria's siege — and among the best-attested figures of the Old Testament.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Hezekiah, king of Judah, is one of its great reformers — he cleanses the temple, destroys idols and high places (even the bronze serpent of Moses, now being worshiped), and keeps a great Passover (2 Kings 18; 2 Chronicles 29–31). When Sennacherib of Assyria invades and besieges Jerusalem, Hezekiah spreads the threatening letter before the LORD and is answered through Isaiah; the Assyrian army withdraws (2 Kings 18–19). Told he will die, he is granted fifteen more years, with the sun's shadow moving backward as a sign (2 Kings 20).

**What history confirms.** Hezekiah is among the best-attested figures of the Old Testament: Sennacherib's own annals describe shutting him up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage" (701 BC), his royal seal impressions (bullae) have been found, and the tunnel he cut to secure Jerusalem's water, with its inscription, still stands (2 Kings 20:20). Marked *attested*.

**On the line of promise.** Hezekiah is a Davidic king on Matthew's genealogy (Matthew 1:9–10), so the gold thread runs through him — the promise carried through a faithful reforming king in a dark century.
readingPointer: His story is told in 2 Kings 18–20.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on 2 Kings 18–20
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Hezekiah"
Diarmaid MacCulloch, Christianity: The First Three Thousand Years

title: Josiah
summary: Judah's last great reformer, who found the Book of the Law in the temple — and died at Megiddo as the end drew near.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Josiah becomes king of Judah as a boy and grows into its last great reformer. When the Book of the Law is found during repairs to the temple and read to him, he tears his clothes in grief at how far the nation has strayed, and launches a sweeping reform — purging idolatry, centralizing worship in Jerusalem, and keeping a Passover unlike any since the days of the judges (2 Kings 22–23). But the reform cannot undo the past, and Josiah is killed at Megiddo confronting Pharaoh Necho (609 BC); within a generation Judah falls.

**Register and history.** Josiah reigned c. 640–609 BC; his reform and his death at Megiddo sit within well-attested history, and his era is firmly anchored (marked *attested*). The Book of the Law found in the temple is widely connected by scholars with Deuteronomy.

**On the line of promise.** Josiah too is a Davidic king in Matthew's genealogy (Matthew 1:10–11), the last reforming king through whom the gold thread runs before the exile.
readingPointer: His reform is told in 2 Kings 22–23.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on 2 Kings 22–23
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Josiah"

title: Jeremiah
summary: The "weeping prophet" who warned of Babylon and lived to see Jerusalem fall — and promised a new covenant.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Jeremiah is called young, in the days of Josiah, to a lifetime of unheeded warning — that Judah's unfaithfulness will bring Babylon down upon Jerusalem (Jeremiah 1). He is the "weeping prophet," beaten, imprisoned, thrown into a cistern, made to wear a yoke as a sign of submission to Babylon; his scroll is cut up and burned by the king (Jeremiah 36). He lives to see Jerusalem fall in 586 BC, and is dragged down to Egypt afterward. Yet at the heart of his book is the promise of a **new covenant** — the law written on the heart, sins remembered no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34).

**Register and dating.** Jeremiah prophesied c. 627–586 BC; his ministry is anchored to well-attested events (the Babylonian conquest), though he is not himself named outside scripture (marked *traditional*).

**His long reach.** The new covenant he promised becomes the New Testament's own name for itself; Jesus takes it up at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20).
readingPointer: Read his call in Jeremiah 1 and the new covenant in Jeremiah 31.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introduction to Jeremiah
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Jeremiah"

title: Ezekiel
summary: Priest and prophet among the exiles in Babylon — of the wheels within wheels and the valley of dry bones.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Ezekiel, a priest, is among the exiles carried to Babylon before Jerusalem's fall, and there he is called by an overwhelming vision — wheels within wheels, full of eyes, and the glory of God above them (Ezekiel 1). His prophecies are strange and dramatic: he lies bound on his side, eats a scroll, sees the glory of the LORD depart from the doomed temple, and in the valley of dry bones watches a dead nation come back to life at God's word (Ezekiel 37). After the fall he turns to hope — a new temple, a new heart, the LORD present again: "The LORD Is There" (48:35).

**Register and dating.** Ezekiel prophesied c. 593–571 BC among the Babylonian exiles (marked *traditional*).

**His place in the story.** He is the prophet of the exile — insisting that God is present even in Babylon, and that resurrection and return are possible for a people that looks dead.
readingPointer: Read the dry bones in Ezekiel 37.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introduction to Ezekiel
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Ezekiel"

title: Daniel
dateDisplay: 6th century BC (traditional) or 2nd century BC (critical dating of the book)
summary: The faithful exile of the lions' den and the apocalyptic visions — and the era's most genuinely contested book.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Daniel is a young Judean noble taken to Babylon, who rises to serve in the courts of Babylon and Persia while refusing to compromise his faith. The first half of his book tells the famous tales — the fiery furnace (his three friends), the writing on the wall, the night in the lions' den — of faithfulness under pagan power; the second half records apocalyptic visions of beasts, kingdoms, and "one like a son of man" coming with the clouds (Daniel 7:13).

**Register, dating, and a real debate.** Daniel is the most contested entry of this era. Traditionally it is read as the work of a 6th-century BC exile. Most critical scholars, however, date the book to the 2nd century BC (c. 165 BC), during the persecution of Antiochus IV, reading its detailed "prophecies" of Greek-era history as written after the fact — while others defend the earlier date. The historicity of its court tales is likewise debated. This entry is marked *contested* to carry that genuine dispute; its canvas position uses the traditional exile setting only for placement.

**Its long reach.** The "son of man" of Daniel 7 becomes Jesus' most characteristic self-designation, and the book's apocalyptic shapes the New Testament's Revelation.
readingPointer: Read the lions' den in Daniel 6 and the son of man in Daniel 7.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introduction to Daniel
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Daniel, Book of"

title: Fall of Jerusalem & the Exile
summary: Babylon burns the temple and carries Judah into exile — the great catastrophe: temple, land, and king lost at once.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** After Josiah, Judah's last kings rebel against Babylon, and Nebuchadnezzar answers: Jerusalem is besieged, taken, and in 586 BC burned — the temple destroyed, the walls broken down, the king blinded and led away, and the people carried into exile in Babylon (2 Kings 25). Lamentations mourns it; Psalm 137 remembers it: "By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down and wept." It is the great catastrophe of the Old Testament — the loss of temple, land, and king all at once.

**What history confirms.** This is firm history: the Babylonian Chronicles record Nebuchadnezzar's capture of Jerusalem, and the destruction layer of 586 BC is visible in the archaeology of the city. Marked *attested*.

**Its meaning.** The exile forces Israel's deepest theological reckoning — how the covenant survives when everything that seemed to guarantee it is gone — and much of the Old Testament takes the shape it has in answer to that question.
readingPointer: Read the fall in 2 Kings 25 and the grief of Psalm 137.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on 2 Kings 25
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Babylonian Captivity"
Diarmaid MacCulloch, Christianity: The First Three Thousand Years

title: Return & the Second Temple
summary: Cyrus lets the exiles go home to rebuild — a humbler restoration, and no king; the promise now hangs on a future son of David.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** When Persia conquers Babylon, King Cyrus decrees that the exiled peoples may return home; the Judeans go back to a ruined Jerusalem and, despite opposition and delay, rebuild the altar and then the temple — the **Second Temple**, completed around 516 BC (Ezra 1–6). Later, under the Persian kings, Ezra returns to teach the Law and Nehemiah to rebuild the city walls (Ezra 7; Nehemiah). It is a smaller, humbler restoration — no king, a modest temple that made the old men who remembered Solomon's weep — but the covenant people and their worship survive.

**What history confirms.** The Cyrus Cylinder attests Cyrus's policy of repatriating deported peoples and restoring their sanctuaries, matching the spirit of the biblical decree; the Persian-period restoration is firm history (marked *attested*).

**Its meaning.** The return proves the exile was not the end. But no Davidic king sits on a throne again in the Old Testament — the promise of an everlasting throne now hangs entirely on a future son of David, and the stage is set for the long wait the New Testament opens into.
readingPointer: Read the decree and the rebuilding in Ezra 1–6.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introductions to Ezra and Nehemiah
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Cyrus"

title: The Minor Prophets
dateDisplay: 9th–5th century BC (the Book of the Twelve)
summary: The Book of the Twelve, minor only in length — the eight shorter prophets gathered here alongside Hosea, Amos, Jonah, and Micah.
article:
**What scripture collects.** The last twelve books of the Old Testament — the **Book of the Twelve**, or Minor Prophets (minor only in length) — gather short prophetic books across some four centuries. Four of the Twelve have their own entries on this canvas: Hosea, Amos, Jonah, and Micah. This entry gathers the other eight: **Joel** (the day of the LORD, the Spirit poured out), **Obadiah** (against Edom), **Nahum** (the fall of Nineveh), **Habakkuk** ("the righteous shall live by his faith"), **Zephaniah** (the day of the LORD), and the three post-exilic voices — **Haggai** and **Zechariah**, who urge on the rebuilding of the temple, and **Malachi**, the last, who closes the Old Testament promising a messenger to prepare the LORD's way.

**Register and dating.** The Twelve span roughly the 9th to the 5th century BC; individually thinly corroborated, and several are of debated date (marked *traditional*). They are grouped here to keep the canvas legible — each is a book in its own right, and will be treated more fully in the biblical-books entries.

**Their long reach.** These small books carry outsized lines: Joel's outpoured Spirit is quoted by Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2), Habakkuk's "the righteous shall live by faith" becomes Paul's and Luther's watchword, and Malachi's promised messenger points toward John the Baptist.
readingPointer: Dip into Joel, Habakkuk, and Malachi — each only a few chapters.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introductions to the Minor Prophets
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Minor Prophets"

title: Esther
summary: The Jewish orphan who became queen of Persia and risked her life to save her people — "for such a time as this."
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, becomes queen of Persia to King Ahasuerus (Xerxes) without revealing her people. When the royal official Haman plots to destroy all the Jews of the empire, Mordecai urges her to intervene — "who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (4:14) — and Esther risks her life before the king to expose Haman and save her people. The deliverance is remembered in the feast of **Purim**.

**Register and dating.** The book is set in the Persian court of the 5th century BC. Its historicity is debated — no Persian record names a Jewish queen Esther, and the book reads to many scholars as a historical novella celebrating deliverance and the origin of Purim; others defend a historical core. This entry is marked *contested*. Notably, the book never once mentions God by name — its providence works entirely behind the scenes.

**Its place.** Esther is one of only two biblical books named for a woman, and a story of courage and hidden providence that has anchored Jewish identity and the joy of Purim ever since.
readingPointer: Read the book of Esther — ten swift chapters.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introduction to Esther
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Esther, Book of"

title: Ezra
summary: The scribe who brought the Law back from Babylon and re-founded Israel around the Torah — a second Moses.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Ezra, a priest and "scribe skilled in the Law of Moses," returns from Babylon to Jerusalem with a commission from the Persian king to teach and enforce the Law (Ezra 7). He is grieved to find the returned community intermarrying and lax, and leads a stern reform; when the Law is read aloud to the assembled people, they weep and then rejoice (Nehemiah 8). Tradition remembers Ezra as a second Moses — the one who re-established Israel around the Torah after the exile.

**Register and dating.** Ezra's mission is placed in the mid-5th century BC (traditionally 458 BC); thinly corroborated outside scripture (marked *traditional*), and the exact relationship of his mission to Nehemiah's is itself debated.

**His place in the story.** Ezra is the great figure of the return to the Law — the shift from temple-and-king to Torah-and-scribe that will shape Judaism through the Second Temple period and into the world of the New Testament.
readingPointer: Read the reading of the Law in Nehemiah 8.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introduction to Ezra
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Ezra"

title: Nehemiah
summary: The cupbearer who rebuilt Jerusalem's walls in fifty-two days — half building, half standing guard.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king, hears that Jerusalem's walls still lie in ruins and asks leave to go and rebuild them. Against mockery and armed opposition from Sanballat and others, he rallies the people to rebuild the wall in fifty-two days — half working, half standing guard, "each labored with one hand and held a weapon with the other" (Nehemiah 4:17). He also reforms the community's social and religious life, canceling the debts crushing the poor.

**Register and dating.** Nehemiah's governorship is placed around 445 BC; his opponent Sanballat is named in the Elephantine papyri, giving his setting external anchorage, so his era is well-placed (marked *traditional*).

**His place in the story.** With Ezra, Nehemiah re-founds the post-exilic community — walls, worship, and law — the last narrated events of Old Testament history before the four centuries of silence the New Testament opens after.
readingPointer: Read the rebuilding in Nehemiah 1–6.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introduction to Nehemiah
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Nehemiah"
